title: How Zorawar Kalra Built a Global Indian Restaurant Empire From His Father's Legacy
excerpt: The son of legendary food critic Jiggs Kalra reveals how he recruited two of India's best young chefs to launch Masala Library — and turned Indian food into a global brand with 50 restaurants and counting.
body:
• Zorawar Kalra's Massive Restaurants now operates roughly 25 Farzi Cafés and a dozen Pa Pa Ya outlets across London, Seattle, Dubai, and India
  • He recruited chefs Himanshu Saini and Saurabh Udinia from Indian Accent — Saini went on to earn the world's first three-Michelin-star Indian restaurant at Tresind Studio in Dubai
  • Masala Library received 300-400 calls daily within three weeks of opening and was booked out for weeks
  • Kalra plans to open 50 restaurants in North America, targeting a market he sees as underserved for casual modern Indian dining

Zorawar Kalra did not grow up in a kitchen, had never worked in a restaurant, and carried zero operational experience when he decided to build what he calls "the best restaurant company in the world." What he did have was a father — the late Jiggs Kalra, known as the "Czar of Indian Cuisine" — and an unshakeable conviction that Indian food deserved better than butter chicken stereotypes.

The Poaching That Started It All

In a candid conversation on Vir Sanghvi's Table 1 podcast, featured by NDTV Food, Kalra addressed the question that has followed him since he launched Masala Library in Mumbai's Bandra-Kurla Complex in 2013: did he steal his chefs from Indian Accent?

"We didn't steal them, we poached them," Kalra said with characteristic directness.

The chefs in question were Himanshu Saini and Saurabh Udinia, then two promising talents in Manish Mehrotra's Indian Accent kitchen. Kalra spotted what he called "the low-hanging fruit" — at a time when only Indian Accent and Bangkok's Gaggan were doing modern Indian food, he recruited the pair to build something new.

"At that time, there were two restaurants in the world that were doing modern Indian food. There was Gaggan, and then we had this wonderful Indian Accent."

— Zorawar Kalra, on the Table 1 podcast

""In about three weeks from the day we opened, we were getting about 300-400 calls a day."

The gamble paid off spectacularly. Saini went on to lead Tresind Studio in Dubai to its third Michelin star, making it the first Indian restaurant in the world to achieve the distinction. Udinia earned recognition from the World's 50 Best Restaurants and the Michelin Guide for his work across multiple Massive Restaurants brands.

From Masala Library to Farzi Café

Masala Library was inspired by a visit to Spain's El Bulli on Kalra's honeymoon, where molecular gastronomy techniques left him wanting to apply them to Indian cuisine. The restaurant was an immediate hit. "In about three weeks from the day we opened, we were getting about 300-400 calls a day. We were sold out for weeks in advance," Kalra told Sanghvi.

But Kalra's real insight was commercial, not culinary. Restaurants like Masala Library and Indian Accent had transformed perceptions of Indian food — but they were expensive and exclusive. What if those same ideas could be served at lower prices in more casual settings?

The answer was Farzi Café, which opened at Delhi's Cyber Hub and was packed from day one. As food writer Vir Sanghvi observed, Kalra had found the sweet spot: "young people from the new middle class, whose palates were used to Indian flavours but who could not bear to go to the old places their parents went to."

He followed Farzi with Pa Pa Ya, which applied the same casual-but-innovative approach to Southeast Asian cuisine, complete with table notes explaining sushi etiquette for first-timers.

A Global Footprint

Massive Restaurants now operates approximately 25 Farzi Cafés and a dozen Pa Pa Ya outlets across London, Seattle, Dubai, the Middle East, and India, according to Sanghvi. The group continues to expand into what were once considered secondary Indian cities — Kanpur, Nagpur — where Farzi Café is often the trendiest restaurant in town.

Kalra's sights are set on North America. The performance of his first U.S. Farzi has convinced him the market is vast and underserved. "Unlike London where there is a lot of casual Indian dining — Masala Zone, Dishoom, Hoppers — that space is wide open in the US and Canada," Sanghvi noted. Kalra's goal: 50 restaurants across the continent.

"He is the man who made Indian food cool for a new generation of diners who had come to associate Indian food with boring restaurants that served Butter Chicken and Dal Makhani."

— Vir Sanghvi, food writer

Carrying Forward a Legacy

The story of Massive Restaurants is inseparable from the story of Jiggs Kalra, who transformed Indian hotel cuisine but never achieved the financial success his contributions deserved. As Sanghvi writes, "Deep down he must remember how his father's health failed. But he must also know that he has achieved far more than Jiggs — who remained sadly unrewarded in his lifetime — could ever have dreamt of."

For Kalra, the mission remains what it was when he started: putting Indian food on the global map. The brands now include MasalaBar, BO-TAI, KODE, and BBQ'D, with a Thai concept and a European seafood restaurant in development. The Delhi Masala Library, which had to close due to landlord issues, is expected to reopen.

Success, Sanghvi observes, has not changed the man — still "high energy, fast-talking, super-optimistic and convinced that his next project will be the best and biggest yet." The difference now is the scale of the canvas.
image_caption: The late Jiggs Kalra, known as the Czar of Indian cuisine, whose culinary legacy his son Zorawar has expanded into a global restaurant empire.
nri_angle: Kalra's plan to open 50 restaurants across North America directly targets the Indian diaspora market, filling a gap in casual modern Indian dining that cities like New York, Toronto, and the Bay Area currently lack.
author: Diaspora Desk
